FIG. 3. (Color online) (a) ALD on a hydroxyl rich polymer surface leads to conformal deposition as shown in the example of Al2O3 ALD growth on cotton (top TEM image). (b) ALD on a polymer surface that lacks reactive functional groups can result in subsurface diffusion and growth within the fiber core, resulting in a less uniform coating at some temperatures. ALD growth on polypropylene at high temperatures (90 /C14 C) results in this kind of subsurface deposition (lower TEM image). Reprinted with permission from Parsons, Atomic Layer Deposition of Nanostructured Materials , edited by N. Pinna and M. Knez (Wiley-VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim, Germany, 2011), pp. 271-300.

FIG. 6. (Color online) Depositing 20 A ˚ of TiN made cotton fabric hydrophobic and helped increase the growth and spread of hADSC cells over a 24 h period. Scale bar ¼ 200 l m. Reprinted with permission from Hyde et al ., Biomed. Mater. 4 , 025001 (2009). Copyright 2009, IOP Publishing.

FIG. 7. (Color online) (a) FT-IR spectra of untreated nylon-6 nanofibers show almost no change after ZnO ALD coating, suggesting little chemical interaction of DEZ with the polyamide material. A subsequent glycidol/TMA MLD layer interacts with the carbonyl and amide modes, although no strong spectral difference is observed if an additional layer of Al2O3 follows the alucone, suggesting the MLD coating protects the nylon nanofibers from further degradation. (b) SEM images of the untreated nylon show that (c) degradation after TMA exposure is (d) minimized with the protective combination of ZnO and glycidol/ TMA coating. Reprinted with permission from Oldham et al ., J. Electrochem. Soc. 158 , D549 (2011). Copyright 2011, The Electrochemical Society.

FIG. 11. (Color online) Patterned ALD ZnO on nonwoven nylon-6 using a compressive metal template. Brown features appear where ZnO has been deposited through the openings in the mask. The middle image shows a sideview of a nonwoven mat stack after ALD, and the bottom image shows the first, second and third nonwoven mat coated in a similar stack. (a) An individual polypropylene fiber with HKUST-1 MOFs and (b) the corresponding fiber mat imaged using an SEM and (inset) optical microscope. The scale bar in the inset is 1 cm. Reprinted with permission from Zhao et al ., Adv. Mater. Interfaces 1 , 1400040 (2014). Copyright 2014, John Wiley and Sons.

FIG. 14. (Color online) Schematic illustration of a spatial ALD reactor for roll-to-roll ALD on textiles. Continuous flow of TMA and water, separated by inert gas inlet ports allow reactants to flow through the porous substrate to the exhaust located under the fiber mat.

tables.caption: TABLE I. Maximum process and glass transition temperatures of several common polymers found in fibers and textiles, however, under extended heating, process temperatures below these maximum values are preferred to maintain the quality of the substrate.
tables.markdown:
TABLE I. Maximum process and glass transition temperatures of several common polymers found in fibers and textiles, however, under extended heating, process temperatures below these maximum values are preferred to maintain the quality of the substrate.

| Material                   | Maximum temperature ( /C14 C)   | Glass transition temperature ( /C14 C)   | References   |
|----------------------------|---------------------------------|------------------------------------------|--------------|
| Cotton                     | 330-360                         |                                          | 86           |
| Nylon-6                    | 220                             | 50                                       | 87           |
| Polypropylene              | 165                             | /C0 10                                   | 88,89        |
| Polyethylene terephthalate | 250-270                         | 67                                       | 90-92        |
| Polybutylene terephthalate | 230                             | 120                                      | 91,93        |
| Polyethylene naphthalate   | 275                             | 120-135                                  | 92           |
| Kevlar V R                 | 540                             |                                          | 94           |
| Polyvinyl alcohol          | 220-230                         | 85                                       | 95,96        |
| Polyacrylonitrile          | 240                             | 95                                       | 97,98        |
| Poly(vinylidene fluoride)  | 160                             | /C0 35                                   | 99,100       |
